items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Irving Mills was the first publisher that was interested in my music... he made the overture to me that he wanted to do this song... other than that song, to which he wrote the lyric, other than that song, I don’t know that he was actually involved in anything else that I wrote other than as the pub

ctx.x: While we’re discussing commercialism versus art, a name must be brought up and it occurs at this time in your career that we’re covering right now, and that’s Irving Mills and your relationship with him and his tying in with your band or with your publishing. What exactly was your connection with Irving Mills, when did it start, and what did it do for you, if anything?

Oh yes, I must certainly say that . . . I can’t say that it didn’t do anything for me, because he was the first person to be interested in my music. As a matter of fact, he came to a club and heard the orchestra playing some sort of . . . I don’t remember what it was, but we had a little riff that we played, out of which I wrote a song called Blues in My Heart, and he heard it. Irving Mills was the first publisher that was interested in my music. I had not even tried to peddle anything, and he made the overture…
You mean he didn’t write all those tunes, huh? [laughs]

items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: I gave it to him for his publishing company ... I sold it to him for $25

ctx.x: Do you remember how it became published? I mean, what were the circumstances of its publication?

I think what happened, I believe I either took it to Irving Mills or I probably made an arrangement for the band and Irving came in the club and heard us play it one night. And showed interest in it, and I gave it to him for his publishing company -- as a matter of fact, I suppose I should say I sold it to him for $25, because that is what I received for it.

And for 28 years I received no further compensation for it -- no royalties, but when the time came around to renew the copyright, I gave it to the same publishing company -- Mills again -- and but this time with a royalty agreement.
